options: developer.salesforce.com
A random blog post
Only Postman's own documentation
This course's own quiz files
questions.explain: developer.salesforce.com hosts Salesforce's official, versioned reference documentation for every API covered in this course.

questions.q: What is Workbench, as described in this lesson?
options: A Salesforce-specific, free, browser-based tool for ad hoc SOQL, REST calls, and simple data loads, independent of Salesforce itself
A required OAuth flow
A Bulk API 2.0 job type
Salesforce's internal metadata deployment engine
questions.explain: Workbench is a free, independent, Salesforce-focused tool for testing queries and REST calls without building a full client app — referenced here by name only, per the course's screenshot policy.

questions.q: What is Salesforce CLI (`sf`) primarily used for?
options: Real-time Streaming API subscriptions only
Metadata deployment, scratch org management, and other API-adjacent developer workflows, built on top of the Metadata API and others
Replacing OAuth authentication entirely
Running SOSL searches only
questions.explain: Salesforce CLI gives developers a command-line layer over APIs like Metadata API for deployment and org management tasks, succeeding the older sfdx command.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend calling GET /services/data/ and /limits rather than hardcoding assumptions about an org?
options: Because hardcoding is always faster and safer
Because these resources let an integration discover the actual supported versions and remaining allocations directly from the org, instead of guessing
Because these are the only two API calls that require no authentication
Because every org has identical versions and limits, making this step optional
questions.explain: Checking these resources directly replaces assumptions with facts about the specific org an integration is talking to, which this lesson calls a habit that prevents production surprises.

questions.q: According to this lesson's course wrap-up, what is the throughline that ran across all 22 lessons when choosing between APIs?
options: Always choose the most powerful API available, regardless of the task
Know what each API is actually for, verify specifics rather than assuming them, and pick the smallest, most appropriate tool for the task at hand
Always default to SOAP for any new integration
Avoid documentation and rely on trial and error
questions.explain: The course's closing framing is deliberately about matching the tool to the task and verifying facts, not reaching for the most powerful or most familiar option by default.
